release.title: Canadian Survey on Business Conditions: Use of artificial intelligence by businesses, second quarter of 2026
release.highlights: In the second quarter of 2026, 19.2% of Canadian businesses used artificial intelligence (AI) in producing goods or delivering services, up from 12.2% in the second quarter of 2025. Over one in seven businesses (14.5%) planned to adopt AI over the next 12 months. Businesses in information and cultural industries (38.6%) and finance and insurance (31.5%) were most likely to use or plan to use AI, while adoption was lowest in mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction (3.4%) and agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting (4.9%). By province, AI use was highest in Ontario (16.8%) and Quebec (15.2%), compared with 8.4% in the Atlantic provinces.

stories.raw_headline: Planned enterprise AI adoption concentrates heavily in virtual agents and text analytics
stories.assumption: Public commentary often assumes businesses planning AI deployment will invest equally across autonomous decision systems and conversational interfaces.
stories.differs_from_daily: The release highlights industry-level adoption percentages without reporting the specific application-type composition among planning firms.
stories.body:
While headline reports focus on the overall adoption rate, the underlying survey reveals sharp divergences in planned tooling.

Specifically, among businesses planning to adopt AI over the next 12 months, 34.8% planned to deploy virtual agents or chatbots, compared with 14.0% for recommendation systems and 13.1% for AI-based decision-making systems. In addition, text analytics (28.5%) and marketing automation (25.6%) also substantially outpaced deep learning (8.9%) and computer vision (3.2%).

As specified in methodology rule M:M2, these figures capture forward-looking adoption intentions over the coming year rather than active systems already in production. This pattern indicates that initial corporate AI expansion remains heavily concentrated in customer-facing and content generation tools rather than embedded operational autonomy.

stories.assumption: Some observers believed business AI deployment plateaued after initial generative AI enthusiasm.
stories.differs_from_daily: The Daily notes both point estimates but does not contextualize the percentage point delta against planned forward intentions.
stories.body:
The release records notable acceleration in active business deployment across Canadian enterprises.

Over the observation window, between the second quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026, the share of Canadian businesses actively using AI rose by 7.0 percentage points, from 12.2% to 19.2%.

Furthermore, active AI deployment outpaced planned adoption intentions by 4.7 percentage points as of the second quarter of 2026.

In accordance with methodology rules M:M2 and M:M3, this expansion reflects percentage point growth between annual cross-sections of active enterprise deployment rather than speculative plans or compounding trajectory assumptions.

stories.title: Subgroup comparison of the regional AI gap: large-enterprise gap is 2.3 points versus 8.4 points overall
stories.headline: Regional AI divide narrows sharply inside large enterprises
stories.raw_headline: Regional AI divide narrows sharply inside large enterprises
stories.assumption: Public commentary often treats headline all-firm provincial differences as evidence of a uniform regional technology deficit.
stories.differs_from_daily: The release highlights top-level provincial adoption percentages without conditioning on enterprise size.
stories.body:
Headline comparisons suggest a wide geographic gulf in Canadian enterprise technology adoption.

At the surface level, across all enterprise sizes, Ontario's AI adoption rate was 16.8% compared with 8.4% in the Atlantic provinces (an 8.4 percentage point margin). However, adoption varies sharply by enterprise scale: nationwide, enterprises with 100 or more employees adopted AI at 38.4%, compared with 10.4% for small businesses with 1 to 19 employees.

When comparing firms of similar scale, among enterprises with 100 or more employees, the gap between Ontario (39.1%) and the Atlantic provinces (36.8%) narrowed to 2.3 percentage points.

In accordance with methodology rule M:M1, this subgroup comparison shows that the regional margin among large enterprises is narrower than the unadjusted all-size gap.

stories.title: Micro-enterprise AI adoption lag driven by information uncertainty rather than outright rejection
stories.headline: Micro-enterprise AI adoption lag driven by information uncertainty rather than outright rejection
stories.raw_headline: Micro-enterprise AI adoption lag driven by information uncertainty rather than outright rejection
stories.assumption: Industry observers often assume that small firms actively resist technology adoption more than large enterprises.
stories.differs_from_daily: The Daily and analytical paper focused on adoption and active non-adoption, omitting the large uncertainty barrier among micro-enterprises.
stories.body:
Public discussions of technology adoption frequently portray micro-enterprises as resistant to innovation.

However, the survey indicates that outright rejection of artificial intelligence is virtually identical across company sizes.

Specifically, rates of active non-adoption remained comparable across scale, with 67.1% of micro-enterprises and 65.8% of large enterprises stating they do not plan to adopt AI.

Rather than deliberate resistance, the decisive barrier facing smaller enterprises is informational uncertainty.

Indeed, businesses with 1 to 4 employees reported an unknown or uncertain status regarding future AI adoption at 31.4%, compared with 15.8% for large enterprises with 100 or more employees.

In accordance with methodology rule M:M2, distinguishing uncertain non-adopters from active rejectors highlights that small-business outreach requires clearer guidance rather than persuasion.

While headline reports focus on the overall adoption rate, the underlying survey reveals sharp divergences in planned tooling.

Specifically, among businesses planning to adopt AI over the next 12 months, 34.8% planned to deploy virtual agents or chatbots, compared with 14.0% for recommendation systems and 13.1% for AI-based decision-making systems. In addition, text analytics (28.5%) and marketing automation (25.6%) also substantially outpaced deep learning (8.9%) and computer vision (3.2%).

As specified in methodology rule M:M2, these figures capture forward-looking adoption intentions over the coming year rather than active systems already in production. This pattern indicates that initial corporate AI expansion remains heavily concentrated in customer-facing and content generation tools rather than embedded operational autonomy.

stories.headline: Regional AI divide narrows sharply inside large enterprises
stories.raw_headline: Regional AI divide narrows sharply inside large enterprises

stories.body:
Headline comparisons suggest a wide geographic gulf in Canadian enterprise technology adoption.

At the surface level, across all enterprise sizes, Ontario's AI adoption rate was 16.8% compared with 8.4% in the Atlantic provinces (an 8.4 percentage point margin). However, adoption varies sharply by enterprise scale: nationwide, enterprises with 100 or more employees adopted AI at 38.4%, compared with 10.4% for small businesses with 1 to 19 employees.

When comparing firms of similar scale, among enterprises with 100 or more employees, the gap between Ontario (39.1%) and the Atlantic provinces (36.8%) narrowed to 2.3 percentage points.

In accordance with methodology rule M:M1, this subgroup comparison shows that the regional margin among large enterprises is narrower than the unadjusted all-size gap.

stories.headline: Micro-enterprise AI adoption lag driven by information uncertainty rather than outright rejection
stories.raw_headline: Micro-enterprise AI adoption lag driven by information uncertainty rather than outright rejection
stories.assumption: Industry observers often assume that small firms actively resist technology adoption more than large enterprises.
stories.differs_from_daily: The Daily and analytical paper focused on adoption and active non-adoption, omitting the large uncertainty barrier among micro-enterprises.
stories.body:
Public discussions of technology adoption frequently portray micro-enterprises as resistant to innovation.

However, the survey indicates that outright rejection of artificial intelligence is virtually identical across company sizes.

Specifically, rates of active non-adoption remained comparable across scale, with 67.1% of micro-enterprises and 65.8% of large enterprises stating they do not plan to adopt AI.

Rather than deliberate resistance, the decisive barrier facing smaller enterprises is informational uncertainty.

Indeed, businesses with 1 to 4 employees reported an unknown or uncertain status regarding future AI adoption at 31.4%, compared with 15.8% for large enterprises with 100 or more employees.

In accordance with methodology rule M:M2, distinguishing uncertain non-adopters from active rejectors highlights that small-business outreach requires clearer guidance rather than persuasion.
